name: Motivated tactician
statement: The motivated tactician is a framework rather than an effect: it holds that people pick among thinking strategies according to their goals, so only its particular predictions can be tested.
meaning: Fiske and Taylor describe five successive pictures of the social thinker: consistency seeker, naive scientist, cognitive miser, motivated tactician and activated actor. Their fourth edition dates the motivated tactician to the 1990s and glosses it as a fully engaged thinker with several cognitive strategies available, who chooses among them, consciously or not, on goals, motives and needs. The claim is about strategy selection, not about a direction of error. It predicts that the same perceiver will sometimes take a shortcut and sometimes think hard, and that a goal manipulation will move which one happens. Nothing in it says whether the resulting judgement will be too harsh, too generous or too confident. Its concrete form is the continuum model of impression formation, in which perceivers start from a category and move towards attribute-based impressions when category fit is poor or motivation is high. That model, and not the label, is what carries testable content.

origin.who: Susan T. Fiske and Shelley E. Taylor
origin.note: Fiske's own curriculum vitae lists Fiske, S. T., & Taylor, S. E. (1991), Social cognition (2nd ed.), New York: McGraw-Hill, the edition the term is normally placed in. That edition was not obtained for this entry, and no source read here shows the phrase inside it. What was read is the authors' fourth edition, which says the 1990s view of the social perceiver 'might best be termed the motivated tactician', and their 2020 retrospective, which calls the Motivated Tactician the second of four phases after the Cognitive Miser. Both cite Fiske's 1992 Journal of Personality and Social Psychology centennial article for the slogan that thinking is for doing. That article is behind a paywall and was checked only against its Crossref record.

evidence: The framework's evidence is the evidence for its members. Neuberg and Fiske ran three experiments in which participants expected to meet a young man formerly hospitalised as a schizophrenic. Short-term, task-oriented outcome dependency led participants to base impressions on the man's particular attributes rather than on the label, and to spend more time attending to those attributes; a third experiment manipulated an accuracy goal instead and produced the same shift. The paper's abstract, which is what was read here, reports no effect sizes. Fiske and Neuberg then set out the continuum model across 74 pages of Advances in Experimental Social Psychology. Fiske and Taylor's own account of the second wave is that it addressed replicability by identifying moderator variables, primarily goals and motivations, and they name interdependence, threat and power as the motives their labs pursued. Two things complicate that account. Kunda and Thagard's meta-analyses put the average effect of individuating information at r = .71 against r = .25 for stereotypes in the absence of individuating information, and they argue that most of the impression-formation findings can be produced by a parallel constraint-satisfaction network requiring little conscious inference. Reynolds and Oakes manipulated interdependence in one experiment and accuracy goals in another, and read their results as showing that whether the salient self-other categorisation is interpersonal or group-based explains variability in impression formation.

replication.headline: No replication of the motivated tactician was located, because there is no motivated-tactician experiment to repeat. The tested claims sit one level down, and they disagree.
replication.detail: Searches for a direct or conceptual replication of Neuberg and Fiske's outcome-dependency experiments, and for a meta-analysis of the continuum model's motivational moderators, returned neither. What exists is a set of neighbouring results. Kunda and Thagard's two meta-analyses, reported inside a theory paper, give individuating information r = .71 and stereotypes r = .25, a gap they use to argue that the serial architecture the continuum model assumes is not needed to fit the findings; the ten pages read here, 284 to 293, carry no study count for either meta-analysis. Lerner and Tetlock reviewed the accountability literature, the most studied motivational moderator of effort, and organised it around the question of when accountability attenuates, does not affect, or amplifies cognitive biases, which is a moderator that runs in three directions. From an adjacent literature outside person perception, a preregistered direct replication tested whether a goal manipulation shifts processing at scale. Roozenbeek, Freeman and van der Linden re-ran Pennycook and colleagues' accuracy nudge for COVID-19 headlines. Their first stage, n = 701, was unsuccessful at p = .67. After a second round, pooled N = 1,583, the treatment by discernment interaction reached uncorrected p = .017, with truth discernment at d = 0.14 in the treatment group and d = 0.10 in the control group, against d = 0.14 and d = 0.05 in the original. The goal manipulation survived and its advantage over the control condition shrank by about half.

limits: The framework does not forbid an outcome. A perceiver who takes a shortcut is a motivated tactician conserving effort, and a perceiver who individuates is a motivated tactician pursuing accuracy, so a single study cannot go against the label, only against a named moderator. That is the cost of the design Fiske and Taylor describe as a response to replicability, and it is why this page maps members rather than issuing a verdict. The search covered Crossref bibliographic queries for replications and meta-analyses of the continuum model and of outcome-dependency impression formation, PubMed, and general web search, and turned up follow-on and neuroimaging work rather than replication attempts. Several documents were not read. The 1991 second edition of Social Cognition is not online in any copy reachable here. Fiske's 1992 article and Fiske and Neuberg's 1990 chapter are paywalled and were checked only against their Crossref records. Reynolds and Oakes was read as its Crossref abstract, which does not say how large their interdependence and accuracy-goal effects were. Carpenter's meta-analysis of the elaboration likelihood model's argument-quality by processing-type predictions bears on the same question of whether motivation moderates depth of processing, and its abstract could not be obtained from the publisher, so no figure from it appears above. The accuracy-nudge replication concerns news sharing, not impression formation, and is quoted here as evidence about goal manipulations in general.
misreadings: Calling it a bias is the first error. It names a model of the perceiver, it predicts no systematic departure from any norm, and a list of cognitive biases is the wrong place to look for it. The second error is treating it as a refutation of the cognitive miser. Fiske and Taylor keep the miser as one setting of the tactician, writing that people are sometimes cognitive misers and sometimes deeper thinkers depending on their purpose. The third is misattributing the miser itself: their fourth edition credits the cognitive miser model to S. E. Taylor's 1981 chapter, not to their own 1984 book, which is where popular accounts usually put it. A fourth error is reading Fiske and Taylor's claim that the approach addressed replicability as a demonstration that it did. Their claim is that specifying goals and motives as moderators makes findings conditional and therefore reproducible, and the accountability literature shows the same moderator producing attenuation, no effect and amplification. Neuberg and Fiske's experiments are also read too widely. They show that outcome dependency and accuracy goals push attention towards a target's attributes in a laboratory task built around a psychiatric label, which is not the same as showing that wanting to be fair defeats a stereotype.
